utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic, and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be long for this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Witness. Your Honours, we don't have any questions. We are satisfied with the answers given yesterday during the examination-in-chief of this gentleman who is testifying today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I don't it will be be long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just want to cover a few areas with you this afternoon. First of all, after you have testified last time, 27th of February this year, you were again contacted by the Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So they contacted you and not you them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object as to relevance. Mr. Waespi wasn't in Court perhaps when the gentleman testified last time but it was made clear prior to the gentleman leaving last time that I would be contacting him because of my inability to continue with my cross-examination because of time constraints. So it was quite obvious. So I object on relevancy grounds as to who contacted whom, knowing that the gentleman would have to come and testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that matters a lot if the Prosecution asks this question for who contact whom. You may proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I take it before giving testimony today you talked to the Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And with the Defence you also discussed the testimony you had given the testimony you had given on the 27th of February; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So there was no discussion about, for instance, the area of responsibility. You didn't discuss that subject with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We just discussed the fact that questions would be directed towards the explanation of the concept and the combat operations carried out by the brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and - I beg your pardon - the instructions for the work of command staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So again my question: You did not discuss the area of responsibility concept with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of the area of responsibility, no, but about combat operations that a brigade engages in as a Infantry Brigade. But as those instructions cover all forms of combat operations and the way in which documents are drawn up in the command, naturally that area of the issue was also included.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let me go to another subject. We have heard testimony here of the presence of General Mladic, General Krstic, Zivanovic in Srebrenica 1995, and I believe you have seen these people as well on the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges how important it is for the senior members of an army to be on the ground, to be present? Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I quite understood your question and the gist of it, but according to the concept and in -- depending on the significance of the assignment, it was normal to expect that the command of the operations and the command of the Drina Corps and the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff or the command of the Main Staff of the VRS as this was the crucial assignment at the time, that they should be on the location where the troops are carrying out their basic assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that will be a fundamental principle, that the senior people would be on the ground where the main effort of an operation take place. I think you called it the crucial assignment.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The main effort of the VRS was to protect and prevent incidents where people in small villages were regularly suffering certain losses and having casualties. In order to prevent that, the operation Krivaja 95 was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's a new exhibit but we won't be using all of it, just one page. It will be Exhibit P860. And the relevant page would be page 9, but if the witness could be shown the whole document. So perhaps he can tell us whether he has seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At least I don't remember seeing it. So I think I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If -- I don't know if this is correct, but it says 1992. We're into 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can explain, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'd like an explanation as to the relevancy, why we're talking about 1992 which is outside the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I haven't read this document yet, and maybe it's a kind of report or regulations or comments, you know, on those regulations, something like this. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking for the relevancy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps the gentleman could explain to us the relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, there is a comment about the activities of the Main Staff, their involvement into what's happening on the ground, what is being done by the brigades. And I would like the witness, who has been called as an expert, to comment on whether that's a valid concept as it was in 1992, 1993, as in 1995. That's what I would like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trivic, can you tell us first of all what this document is about. And I think it's probably enough to look at the first page of the document, the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When anyone is asked to look at a hundred-and-more page document in a couple of minutes and to assess it as you are requesting -- I do not wish to be rude, but I don't think it is appropriate. In any event, I can say that the title is "Analysis of the Combat Readiness and Activities of the Army of Republika Srpska," which shows what it is. It is an analysis of combat readiness for 1992. That is the year when the army was formed. In any event, any analysis requires one to be able to compare it with something that constituted a basis for its activities, for its formation, and everything else. And essentially this analysis, which I haven't read -- I've already said that I don't remember, in fact I'm quite sure that I didn't read it, in 1992 I didn't take part in this analysis, so I never received this document to be able to make any conclusions from it regarding my own unit. But in any event, an analysis should contain what are the basic premises for the formation of the army of Republika Srpska was made the best of, how the army was formed, what the response to replenishment of units was since in 1992 there was a deviation from the concept by the people who did not wish to respond to the call-up and join the units of the VRS. So the army was being formed by replenishment --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't want to cut you short. I don't want you to give an analysis yourself about that. I just have a brief comment to make, and I believe it's not necessary for you to give any comment except for the part we are discussing. The only thing I would like to ask you is to turn to your version, page 133. And in English it's page 153. So we see who signed this document and perhaps also the date so it's on the record. Mr. Trivic, can you tell us? Hundred and thirty-three. If you could read out date and -- and who authored this document.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 5th of April, 1993, and the signatory of the document is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic. Now let's go to just one paragraph. It's on page 9 in both versions, Your Honours, Mr. Trivic. In the English version it's the second paragraph from the top, and I do have a -- well, I believe we have one for the ELMO. The second paragraph from the top. And in your version, Mr. Trivic, it's the second paragraph from the bottom. And I would just like to read you this part of it and if you need more, you can certainly acquaint yourself. I read the last sentence of that paragraph: "The involvement of different staff bodies in the brigades and other units yielded particularly good results because in that way directives, commands and orders reached those who were to execute them in the fastest way possible -- the fastest possible way, and the planned concerted action was relatively quickly performed." Now, does that confirm what you said before about the importance of the presence of Main Staff people?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I wasn't able to follow you. I didn't find this passage on page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's the last paragraph, and it's the last sentence in this last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my language it is not on page 9. I can't find the beginning of the sentence as you read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The beginning, I think, in your language of the second paragraph to the last from the bottom starts: "We devoted significant attention to controlling and extending assistance to subordinated commands." That's the beginning of the paragraph I'm quoting.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To controlling and extending assistance to subordinate commands."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Devoting special attention to them."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you go to the last sentence on that paragraph which starts with: "The involvement of different Main Staff bodies in the brigades," and so on. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, my question is whether that's a confirmation of what you said before about the importance of Main Staff personnel being on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This cannot be identified with what I said. This is an analysis of combat readiness of the army in 1992 for which it was absolutely essential and necessary for organ of the Main Staff to go to the units in view of the need to set up those units and revive those units so as to form defence zones. This was the beginning of the functioning of the Army of Republika Srpska. In 1995, the reasons were quite different, and a great deal of effort was required in those days to activate the population that did respond to the call-up and who was confronted with various dangers in various parts of Republika Srpska. Those units had to be formed, a light infantry brigade, or infantry brigades formed with the personnel left over to fill in the posts, because the vast majority of the Muslim and Croat population did not respond to the mobilisation of Territorial Defence units which were developed into light infantry brigades. And the one we are talking about throughout the war remained a light infantry brigade, and no one can say that it didn't develop from a TO unit which had its plan of engagement with the highly qualified personnel. However, in this case the criteria for the replenishment of units was not as they used to be when the best people were sent to the units. In this particular case, the numbers had to be satisfied, and even those who were unfit for the army joined. So for 1995, this paragraph is not applicable. This related to the formation of units, assistance to people to for those units, whereas in 1995 the importance of the presence of superiors had to do with the execution of assignments given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Trivic. Let's go to a couple of regulations. If you could be shown the brigade rules of 1984. That's Prosecution Exhibit 370. Now, have you seen these rules before?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the other rules you have been discussing yesterday, I think that was the manual for the work of commands and staff, and for the record that was Exhibit D84, you told us that these principles were applied by the VRS in 1995, the regulations about the work of command staff. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The manual for commands and staffs was used to prepare combat documents and for the work of the commands on the basis of those provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this other set of rules, the brigade rules of 1994, were they also applied by the VRS in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And similarly, if the witness could be shown the next exhibit. This is Exhibit P379, "Regulations on the Application of International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY". I just have the same question as before. Were these regulations also applied by the VRS in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it can be returned. Now, let's conclude with the area of responsibility. In your earlier testimony in February 2004, in your direct examination by Mr. McCloskey, he did not ask you a question about the area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let me --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let me read that to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's on page 7493.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'll read out slowly what Mr. McCloskey asked you on 27th of February. "Do you know what army units were supposed to cooperate with the MUP to secure those roads from the Muslim army?" And your answer: "The units which were in that area which were engaged in the area within their area of responsibility. The Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade were definitely tasked in this way, and they drew their own conclusions of what it was that they were supposed to do in accordance with that order." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, yes, and thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You're welcome. Then Mr. Karnavas, in cross-examination, followed up on it. And I'll read from page 7516.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Okay. Now, in your position did you have a zone of responsibility?" "Yes, I did."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Now, was that zone of responsibility based on the rules, the brigade rules?" Your answer: "In this case, no. The area was much broader than the brigade would be assigned to in accordance with the rules." Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That was in February. Now, yesterday, a couple months later, you were asked almost verbatim the same questions by Mr. Karnavas, and I'll quote: "Now, first of all," Mr. Karnavas asks, "does the brigade have a zone of responsibility such as the one that's reflected on that document?" And I believe you were talking about the map. And your answer is: "The brigade does not have a zone of responsibility. It's not formulated as a zone of responsibility in terms of any task or aspect of combat activity." Do you remember having said that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How can you explain almost the same answer -- the different answer to the same question?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that all military analysts -- and I am not a military analyst, I'm just a professional soldier who took part in the war and started the rules and implementation and concept of the war -- would find it clear. Yesterday, I had a document in front of me, and at my previous appearance in court there was no document. It was just a discussion about the zone of responsibility of a brigade, which is normally done. Yesterday, I had a document in front of me which I still claim as a combat document does not exist and is not drafted. There is a decision of the brigade commander representing a zone with elements of combat deployment, grouped forces, and it is signed by the person who drafted it. And it is updated every day and in time generally. So the document that I was shown yesterday does not exist in a brigade. However, if you insist, the term that is used in a discussion, regardless of combat documents as a reflection of the order and the instructions for a logbook, if we're talking about a zone of responsibility that is assigned to a particular body, the only organ that does have its zone of responsibility in the brigade command and higher commands is the intelligence organ, and for them an area of intelligence responsibility is assigned. And now let me refer to yesterday's map. That map was possible only since someone drew it up according to someone's instructions or request. The only possibility is that it was formed in 1992 while General Zivanovic was still a colonel, while the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina had still not split up, and when in the settlements in Bratunac, Srebrenica municipality or any other municipality with mixed populations, the intelligence organs who monitor the situation in various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given the task to prepare some kind of auxiliary documents with a zone of responsibility, but nobody actually formalised this. When the population moved from one area to another, when defence zones were formed and defence lines in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then the brigades were formed out of people who responded. On the one hand there was one nation, on the other another, and they each had their zones of defence. So I hope I have made myself clear. The term one use in a discussion is one thing, and the document I was shown yesterday prompted me to give the answers I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Trivic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any redirect, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, if we were to go into the brigade rules - and I don't have them in front of me but that would be P370 - would you find in those rules something that you referred to as an area of intelligence responsibility that more or less reflects a geographical region such as the map itself?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go back to the rules, the brigade rules, focusing now on the intelligence and security sectors. Is there a specific language regarding an area or zone of responsibility for those organs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only as an area of intelligence responsibility that is supposed to be monitored by the intelligence organ who is in charge for that area. In order to make the document valid, this intelligence organ has to indicate its observation points, axes of patrol, recording of phenomena that is necessary for certain intelligence organs but also records that include a certain legend which explains where ambushes were made, how many people were arrested, et cetera. But the document I was shown yesterday did not indicate even that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sticking with the rules now. Now, if we went to the rules, would we find anything in those rules that would designate to a brigade zones of responsibility such as the one that we saw in the rules, such as the one that's reflected in the map?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What sort of zones, just again, are we going to find in the rules which you've indicated to a previous answer from Mr. Waespi were applicable at the time? What sort of zones are reflected in the rules for brigades?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The zone of defence and the zone of offensive or assault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again so we have a clear definition, could you please tell us what a zone of defence is, what it looks like. At least -- and I'm speaking based on the rules.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the rules, a zone of defence is a piece of land limited or outlined by at least four points. These four points have to be landmarks, features, easily observable that connect the right side with the most prominent points of the front line of defence, the left side, and the area behind the lines, the depth. That is a zone of defence only when all the elements of combat disposition of a unit are indicated in it, the neighbours, as in a combat document, left neighbours, right neighbours, and the time when this zone of defence is drawn into a map in that form with the approval and signature of the person who created the map, when the map was started, when it was completed, for which period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one final question. During the events surrounding Srebrenica, your particular brigade, what sort of a zone did it have for those events?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part of the assignment, there was action - and I cannot remember it off the cuff - with a part of the forces of the Skelani Battalion on the axis that separates the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves outlined by four points which we can see from the order of the commander of the operation or the corps commander. When the prerequisites had been created and when it was estimated that action can be corrected from that axis, then the next assignment was in the north-west parts of the populated area of Srebrenica, again marked by four limiting points. The assignment was to carry out an operation and to emerge at the next lines. All this was accompanied by orders and corrections in the decision both in the textual, in the graphic parts. And since the forces of the 28th division were retreating, the current assignment then was formulated as search of the terrain. But in adequate military terminology, that is called pursuit. At the time when the enemy is crushed and is in retreat, the forces that had carried out the operation move into pursuit in order to catch up with the enemy. And that was the part of the assignment in which my brigade, that is part of my brigade, was involved. In all the three stages there was an area of operation, and I would have to look at the documentation which is necessary for quality command and leadership of the forces of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Yes. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes. I have only one question. It's about this famous map that we have heard was not drafted or made according to the rules and doesn't represent anything, as you said, but we had one witness coming here and telling us that this map was hanging on the wall of the duty officer place in the Bratunac Brigade. Can you tell me why a useless and let's say not-according-to-the-rules map was hanging in the duty officer's position in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be free to give you an indirect answer since you formulated your question in this way, that is, requiring an answer with an explanation. I saw that map in 1993 when I first came to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. The commander then was Colonel Vuksic. That same map was hanging on the wall, and who made that map and with what reason, I don't know. I suppose it was made at the time of the events which are described when talking to the Prosecutor, that is at the time when it was necessary to record certain movements before the split-up, before the basic prerequisites were created for the establishment of the Bratunac Brigade. When I said that it did not represent anything, the simple explanation for that answer is that the map does not contain anything that would make it possible to use it as a document. It does not even indicate the command post of the brigade, which would be a necessary element for any graphic depiction of the situation of the brigade. If at least that element had been recorded, we could talk about that map as a valid document, but this way it does not have the necessary contents that would make it a combat document. Somebody drew it up on the basis of the rules which stipulate how a map is drawn and that is all. It does not contain the necessary elements for a document of the kind that we are discussing here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you, but that was not my question. My question was why a useless map was hanging in the office, in the duty officer's office.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any duty officer's room, there was a map of the territory where that particular command was located. In certain units it was represented as the working map. A working map has different content. It is made for a longer period. The initial and the current situation of the combat disposition is indicated, and that map is constantly updated. At the time when the replenishment of the units was made from leftover forces, it is possible that that map - and this is only my assumption - that that map was drawn up by somebody who was designated to act as an intelligence officers at the time when the Bratunac municipality and Srebrenica municipality and that entire area were still populated the way they were in 1992. If somebody did it based on the intelligence plan of the brigade from the time when the Bratunac Brigade was established, if somebody drew up that map with the idea that later developments would be recorded on it and that it be used for orientation - and I already indicated that I arrived only later - then that map could have been used only as an ordinary topographic map depicting that entire territory without any indications of zones of responsibility, combat disposition, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you mean to say it was a sort of decoration, standing -- hanging there for three years?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There was not enough map or sections of to have graphic maps in that area, so we did with what was available. And this map could have served as an aid for orientation for the people who worked in that area. That was its purpose. The commander could have used it to show certain axis, directions, as a topographic map. And I personally used it when Colonel Vuksic was showing which routes could be used to get to the adjacent area of Sekovici, Konjevic Polje, et cetera, and what the distances were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Argibay. Any questions out of the Judge's questions? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like to tender D200 and D201, and as is reflected in the list of exhibits here, the translation is pending. So tentatively, assuming that we get the translation, if I could have a week or so. I don't think it would be that much more to have the translations done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we still don't have -- well, we have the B/C/S now, I see. But I believe to -- to ask for the introduction into evidence of a whole book, even if it's translated, and I question the use of resources of this book at this time. I believe he read it out and so we can live with that. He gave his explanation. I don't think it's necessary to have the whole book introduced into evidence, frankly. The same applies to the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Here's my response to that: First of all, with the first book "Strategy of Armed Combat," I'm told that the entire book was given to be translated. It is an official document that was used at the time. We thought that it would be useful, so nothing is taken out of context. They don't have to read the entire book, but certainly it's there and it's available, and it was used at the time. The second document, which was the introduction to the "Theory of Military Management," though it was used, and particularly as far as training was concerned, there was a small portion from which the witness replied on explaining some of his answers yesterday. Again, we think this is also relevant both to the case, also relevant to understanding military principles. It's -- I think few of us in this courtroom are versed enough in those matters. So I don't think that in any way it taxes or overburdens the already overburdened, you know, list of exhibits that we have. I think it's useful, and I don't see why we shouldn't at least make it available to everybody, especially to the members of the Bench. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, there are a lot of books and publications concerning the armed conflicts in the former Yugoslavia during that era. I think the Tribunal cannot admit and translate all those books into English and have them admitted. That's the problem. What if we admitted this book, with the relevant parts? As for how much, the relevant parts, I think we will rely on the submission of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Pending the translation, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. That will be just fine, Your Honour. I just want to make sure you don't have -- when you're trying to figure it all out, I didn't translate a particular chapter. You don't have it available. So I want to make sure that it's all available. But that's a fair ruling, Your Honour, and we accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Those two documents are admitted into evidence withal relevant parts. And on the part of the Prosecution, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, just a remark. Of course we accept your ruling, but we have some debate about the report of the Dutch government. Just a hundred pages was referenced numerous times and we didn't admit it. And here comes -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we made a decision that eventually it will come into evidence. We'll see how relevant those documents is. But please remind us at the end of the Defence case how many documents are pending at that moment and then we'll consider it at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, there's another matter I would like to bring to the attention of both parties. During the testimony of this witness, we admitted six documents under seal, and those six documents could be separated into categories. One is the video clip, and the other is the diary of this witness. So if we lift the confidentiality of the witness for the transcript for the last testimony, it seems to me there is no need for the protective measures, you know, for those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, for the diary, I would submit, Your Honour, with all due respect that they should be kept on a confidential basis, because I believe -- and I don't think they translated all of it. And we haven't received the entire translation, but I think that this was a personal document. It wasn't an official document. There were other matters on the diary that were of a personal nature. So I would prefer that it remain confidential, and of course I'm willing to work with the Prosecution to see what portions are innocuous enough to be open to the public. But I think the safe ruling at this point in time would be to keep it on a confidential basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any view?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with Mr. Karnavas, and perhaps the witness could also identify the areas which he deems are really private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So I believe that the video clips --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the video clips is not tendered at this stage, so we do not discuss this matter. As for the diaries, especially personal diaries, we'll see, you know, which part should be still in the protective measures and certain parts we should lift the confidentiality of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just -- just while I remember. There was some personal thoughts with respect to certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course, those are, I think, highly confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so I certainly would object - not that I can do anything about it - but I will object to those being open to the public. I think they will be -- the gentleman was kind enough to bring the diary to start and we commend him for that. But I think those private thoughts should be kept private. Now, with respect to dates, places, obviously we don't have a problem with that. But private thoughts, particularly about certain personalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I hope the parties could meet together to discuss this issue and submit us a suggestion concerning the diary. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's very agreeable, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we still have a few minutes left. Mr. Karnavas, would you please brief us about the upcoming witnesses next week or the week after next?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Next week -- okay. Next week we have two, possibly three witnesses. The -- do you want the names, Mr. President, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe some of them are in -- have the protective measures, so you don't have to mention the names. If there is a necessity, we could go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- unless you want to hear the names, Your Honour, I don't. But basically what it comes down to is this: We have two, possibly three witnesses next week. The following week we have Professor Radovanovic, who is our expert on demographics. He's prepared a report. We hope to have it translated by Monday. It's been in the works. It's been in the works. It's 25 pages. I anticipate that she will require two days of testimony, because she spent a lot of time going through the methodology used by Mr. Brunborg. We've had her here. She's gone through the document. The OTP was kind enough to allow her access to their computers and she came with some assistance and has put a tremendous amount of time in that. After that I anticipate we will have Mr. Karremans testifying on the 24th and 25th. He will not be able to make it next week. And we've been in contact so in accommodating his schedule, it will be 24th and 25th. We did have a military expert on our list. I spoke with Mr. McCloskey, and I had indicated to him that perhaps I would wait until Monday for him to give the update to the Court, although I'm willing to give it. We reached an accommodation, basically - and he can correct me on Monday, or Mr. Waespi can - that they do not have any objections to the report and at attachment to the report that we filed, the supporting material, for it to be coming in in lieu of live testimony. They don't accept the contents, obviously. That's for the Trial Chamber to decide. But at least it would very much as a 92 -- or an expert report coming in. So that would save us two or three days of testimony. So we believe -- we believe that we will finish on time provided that Mr. Karremans stays -- that we can keep it within the two-day limit and that's what I'm hopeful. I tried to get him a little bit earlier. But in any event two witnesses next week, possibly three. If the third witness comes up I don't expect him to be more that a two-session witness. And frankly, we could use the added time in between for preparation. And as you know, we have been going at it at a fairly rapid clip. In the final week they're pretty important witnesses. So even though we will probably not sit for couple of days next week, I think it's important for us to have that additional time. So that's what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So how many witnesses altogether in the future two weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maximum five, minimum four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So you still remember that the deadline for your case is on the 25th of this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, but I've also, Your Honour, haven't lost sight of the fact that the Jokic case is not to start on the immediate Monday. I just -- you know, I have to take advantage of every opportunity I get to just sort of indicate my awareness of these things, Your Honour. I hope that we end on the 25th. You know, I could not get the gentleman earlier in light of the circumstances, and again, this is -- these are terribly difficult and complex issues that I'm dealing with, lots of prep time, and I don't want to complain, but this week I think we've been extremely flexible in light of the circumstances. There is one other outstanding subpoena, and we've been in contact with the Serbian government. They're going to try to assist. I'm not holding out on that. If the gentleman is not available by that time, he's just not available. We'll see what we have to do if something comes up later on. But that's where we are, Your Honour. So I anticipate resting on the 25th, but again, Mr. Karremans may take a little longer. It's a very complex issue. The gentleman has never really testified, and I think that there are some issues that need to be clarified in this case. So that's where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple of points. Military expert, that's true. It was discussed with Mr. McCloskey, and that's what -- he is correct in the assessment, but I'm sure Mr. McCloskey will address you on Monday and sort of give his final okay. We would appreciate getting the third witness, the name of the third witness next week as soon as possible. We have the two names but not the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The third one is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Shall we go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please, if we are going to mention the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We are in the open session. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to conclude two other points. 92 bis, that's correct, we accept testimony of about -- I think they filed 28 witness statements, and we accepted all of them but five. So for five of these witnesses we would require their attendance for cross-examination. And the expert on demographics, Professor Radovanovic, the rules really give us 30 days or, I believe, a time indicated by the Trial Chamber, and does he see with the expert report of the military witness if we have time to look at it, we may even say the report can come in. So -- but it's a difficult topic, as Mr. Karnavas indicated, and we need time to read it, to discuss it with our people. And I can't do that before I have it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just so I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just so we understand this whole concept about equality of arms. When it takes me two or three months to get folks motivated in the Registry to assist, and for me to file request and request to get the funding, to arrange the travel, and then this professor came here, and then even though we had prior notice there was a glitch. I haven't complained, but I brought her here with two assistants, and there was a lot of down time waiting to get access to the computers. So we can't have it both ways where on the one hand it frustrates the Defence by not having the resources or everything is delayed by weeks on end, and at the same time be inflexible and keep to the rules. Now, I understand that this professor has looked at the work that's been performed by the Office of the Prosecution. They have an ton of experts. In facts, they have an entire section on this. I agree with Mr. Waespi. It's a rather complex issue. But the report is about 25 pages. It's not very large. That's number one. Number two, she has testified before the Tribunal, so she's not an unknown and -- you know, they know her. She's testified in other cases. If fact, I'm told she's made an impression on the Prosecution. Number three, she will be arriving a couple of days earlier. If they wish to give up a Sunday, for instance, or part of a Sunday, I certainly will make sure that Professor Radovanovic is available to meet with them so they can discuss her report in assisting them in preparing for their cross-examination, something that was never available to the Defence. So again I just want to point out the -- you know, if we're going to be fair in this process, we have to understand that the Defence has certain limitations, and I could not engage this expert until we had Brunborg on the stand. What he's finished testifying, I then put a series of steps in motion, and I have the documentation to demonstrate the amount of effort that I've gone through in personal expenses -- personal -- in order to have her come here with her expert. So we've done everything that's humanly possible. And she's going to be testifying for approximately two days, for both sides, that is. I anticipate one day for the Defence, perhaps one day for the -- and again I will make the professor available to the Prosecution. If Sunday is not a convenient day, I'll make her available on Saturday. Not a problem. They can speak with her, go over the report, talk with her. I think that's a generous offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this Bench has already given you instructions of how to conduct the direct examination with the expert witness. I doubt very much whether up need for the whole day to ask questions to the expert. But I hope you just bear that in mind, and of course this is your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm bearing it in mine. I'm also bearing that I sat through five days of Butler, five excruciating days where I wasn't even able to object. So you can imagine the level of my frustration, but I sat there. I'm asking for one day. And It's a complex issue. And I'm sure you will be riveted, riveted with the direct examination and the information that we will get from Professor Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question about 92 bis witnesses. I think this Trial Chamber is just considering the filings from the Defence as well as the reply from the Prosecution. We are going to make a decision concerning of those witnesses early next week. The third issue about the videolink witnesses in Mr. Jokic's case, and the Bench is considering this possibility, and if there is any, the decision will be rendered next week, because we need at least two weeks for preparation. And as for the Pre-Defence Conference for Mr. Jokic's case, I wonder if next week we will only have two witnesses could we have the Pre-Defence Conference fit in somewhere next week? Is it possible, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite frank, Your Honour, I had planned to spend next week in Zvornik to finalise the preparations for all the witnesses that we have announced and to complete my interview with the military expert. So it would be more acceptable for us if we could hold it at some other time. But if you feel that it is absolutely essential, maybe I should postpone my trip there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we should do our best to help you to finish your investigation. I just make a suggestion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, finally I have to say that this Trial Chamber is very grateful to the government of the Netherlands for their assistance in calling a witness to testify in this case, especially to the Ministry of Defence as well as the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. In the past, they gave us a lot of help, but we just take it as granted, but now, I think as well as Mr. Karnavas, are very grateful for their assistance. I think that is all for today, and next Monday we'll sit in Courtroom III at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of June, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
